extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, journalism students, and media practitioners interested in solutions/constructive journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Produce news reporting that focuses on responses to social problems, explaining how and why those responses work (or fail), anchored in evidence. The guidance covers what to emphasize in coverage, common pitfalls, and a production rule-of-thumb for balancing problem vs. solution material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous, evidence-based reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions journalism is rigorous, evidence-based reporting on the responses to social problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should be anchored in credible evidence; proponents argue an evidence-based approach distinguishes solutions journalism from mere 'good news' reporting and diminishes risk of bias. Avoid relying on untested theories or superficial descriptions of responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify root causes of the social problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions stories identify the root causes of a social problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should go beyond symptoms to explain underlying causes so readers understand why the problem arose and how the response addresses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominently highlight the response(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions stories prominently highlight a response, or responses, to that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The response(s) should be a central element of the story (not just an anecdotal aside); emphasis tends to be on the innovation or intervention rather than primarily on a person or institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present evidence of the impact of the response
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions stories present evidence of the impact of that response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show empirical or credible evidence that the response has had an effect. Evidence distinguishes solutions journalism from feel-good pieces and supports claims about effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how and why the response is working or not
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should explain how and why the response is working, or not working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide causal or mechanistic explanation so readers understand the conditions under which the response succeeds or fails; include contextual factors and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When possible, provide insight into complex systems
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, solutions stories present an insight that helps people better understand how complex systems work, and how they can be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond isolated examples to illuminate system-level dynamics and transferable lessons for readers, communities, and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess responses that are working today (not untested theories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions stories assess responses that are working today, as opposed to untested theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize real-world, implemented solutions with observable outcomes rather than speculative or hypothetical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the innovation rather than the individual or institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions journalism tends to place more emphasis on the innovation than on a person or institution responsible for that innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid centering pieces on hero narratives; instead, focus analysis on what the intervention is and how it operates so it can be evaluated or replicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial 'good news' reporting (no feel-good or hero worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not devolve into 'feel-good' storytelling or hero worship; avoid a superficial presentation of a response without careful analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include upbeat 'good news' sections that highlight positive anecdotes without examining effectiveness, limitations, or evidence. Critics warn such coverage can be simplistic and driven by revenue/advertising motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advocacy and calls to action; maintain journalistic objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions stories should not cross into advocacy or be connected to a 'call to action' for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an evidence-based, critical stance to reduce bias. Supporters argue that rigorous evidence and critical examination help distinguish reporting from advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance coverage between problem and solution (two-thirds rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule of thumb: no more than one-third of the paper should describe the problem, while at least two-thirds should be devoted to solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This production guideline (used by the publication Solutions) is a concrete heuristic for story structure and emphasis; adapt as appropriate to context and editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the need for subject-matter expertise to avoid oversimplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Many complex social issues do not have clear causes or clear solutions; pursuing solutions stories may require considerable expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should be cautious about oversimplifying systemic problems; when covering technical or complex topics, consult experts and present limitations so stories do not mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solutions journalism to complement traditional watchdog reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions journalism augments and complements the press' traditional watchdog role by presenting evidence that entrenched problems can be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame solutions reporting as part of the broader journalism ecosystem—use it to inform citizens and strengthen the impact of investigative work, not to replace accountability reporting.
